# When tree search wins validation but loses on test: a bounded AI Scientist v2 experiment

**AI disclosure: ChatGPT authored this article and the experiment reused part of Sakana AI's AI Scientist v2 code. This is not an automatically generated manuscript from its native pipeline.**

An automated research system has to answer two distinct questions: which experiment to run next, and whether the resulting claim generalizes. We reused a small piece of the official AI Scientist v2 implementation to compare tree-guided and random exploration under the same candidate-evaluation budget. Tree search improved validation loss but slightly worsened loss on a held-out segment. The negative result is worth preserving.

![Cover: 160 candidate evaluations and 10 paired searches](/assets/research/ac03v2-cover.svg)

## How v2 explores research ideas

The [2025 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08066) describes a system that reduces dependence on human-authored templates. An experiment manager coordinates baseline development, hyperparameter tuning, improvement, and ablation studies. Multiple initial drafts are developed into a tree, and failed nodes can be repaired. One of three generated manuscripts reached the acceptance threshold in the authors' ICLR 2025 workshop experiment. That is an important demonstration, not proof that every generated claim is scientifically valid.

At the pinned official revision 96bd51617cfdbb494a9fc283af00fe090edfae48, the configuration specifies four workers, three initial drafts, a 0.5 debugging probability, a maximum debugging depth of three, a 3,600-second execution timeout, and stage-specific iteration limits of 20, 12, 12 and 18. Candidate selection normally uses an LLM; the Journal also has a metric-only branch. We reused only that branch.

![The native workflow and the limited component executed here](/assets/research/ac03v2-pipeline.svg)

## A small, measurable search problem

We used 1,115,394 characters of actual Tiny Shakespeare text. The SHA-256 is 86c4e6aa9db7c042ec79f339dcb96d42b0075e16b8fc2e86bf0ca57e2dc565ed. The contiguous first 80% forms the training split, the next 10% validation, and the final 10% test. The vocabulary is derived from training only, with an unknown-character slot, for 66 symbols. All validation and test targets after the first two characters are scored. The test segment was excluded from selection in this experiment, but had been used for validation in our earlier v1 experiment; it is not untouched at the research-program level.

For an order-k character n-gram, the preceding k characters form a context c. Additive smoothing gives the next-character probability (count(c,x)+alpha)/(count(c)+alpha*V), where V is the vocabulary size. Small alpha emphasizes observed counts; large alpha pulls the distribution toward uniform. The score is mean negative log likelihood (NLL), so lower is better.

We fixed a grid of 24 candidates: context order 0, 1 or 2 crossed with eight smoothing constants (0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30). Both policies evaluate the same three roots at alpha=1, then five distinct new candidates. Tree search expands an unvisited neighboring alpha of the best expandable node. Random search chooses from the remaining grid. The candidate counts match; actual wall-clock time and compute cost are not controlled. Ten paired random seeds determine exploration. Selection uses only validation NLL, and only the chosen candidate is scored on test.

We extracted the reviewed metric-only branch of Journal.get_best_node from the pinned upstream file. The search policy around it and the n-gram implementation are our bounded experiment. This is not the native four-stage agentic tree-search system.

## The negative result

![Measured validation and test NLL](/assets/research/ac03v2-loss.svg)

| Policy | Validation NLL | Test NLL |
|---|---:|---:|
| Tree | 2.023641 | 2.163059 |
| Random | 2.042117 | 2.160495 |

Tree search improved validation NLL by approximately 0.905%, yet its mean test loss was 0.002564 higher. It won one paired test comparison, tied three and lost six. All ten tree searches selected order 2 with alpha 0.1; random search selected alpha 0.01, 0.1 or 1 at order 2. We replayed all 160 candidate evaluations, and all recorded values matched except runtime.

The seeds vary exploration on one corpus, not independent datasets. No significance or broad generalization claim follows. A stronger experiment would use a previously untouched corpus, pre-register the search space and budgets, and repeat with independent tasks. In particular, the fact that random search found a slightly better test model does not justify tuning on the test set.

## What Anicca can reuse

A narrow ManagerBench evidence gate checks missing or duplicate candidates, fixed budgets, parent ordering, validation selection and finite metrics. Seven tests cover valid and invalid records. Promotion remains false: validation improvements cannot substitute for independent evidence. No Manager weights were trained and no mobile app changes or user benefits were measured.

The official system targets Linux and CUDA, requires model APIs, and executes generated code. Our Mac had approximately 1.4 GiB of free storage, and neither an isolated generated-code runner nor an authorized API budget was established. We did not run the native launch_scientist_bfts.py, idea generation, repairs, writing or automated review. The current source license requires explicit AI disclosure and restricts uses including personal-attribute inference; we do not transfer the code into those applications.

Sources: [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08066), [pinned upstream repository](https://github.com/SakanaAI/AI-Scientist-v2/tree/96bd51617cfdbb494a9fc283af00fe090edfae48), [Tiny Shakespeare](https://github.com/karpathy/char-rnn/tree/6f9487a6fe5b420b7ca9afb0d7c078e37c1d1b4e/data/tinyshakespeare). Full native reproduction, independent evaluation and publication remain tracked in [issue #806](https://github.com/Daisuke134/anicca-ops/issues/806).

Research automation should optimize independently verified discoveries, not merely the best validation score seen during a search.
